mn41.setting: Sālā, a brahmin village of Kosala. The brahmin householders ask why some beings go to a bad destiny and some to a good one.
mn41.brief:
Because of unrighteous conduct in ten ways, and righteous conduct in ten:
- three of body: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, or abstaining
- four of speech: lying, divisive, harsh and idle speech, or abstaining
- three of mind: covetousness, ill will and wrong view, or their opposites
teaching: The ten wholesome courses of action (dasa kusala kammapatha) are the moral foundation under every other teaching in this book.
mn41.living: **The ten are the three doors.** This sutta is the canonical source of the body, speech and mind framework in the Rubric. Note the first mental fault: wanting what belongs to another. Covetousness about wealth is the root error the money suttas guard against.

notes.text: "Covetous": the sutta defines it as coveting another's wealth: "Oh, if only their belongings were mine!" The first fault of mind is about money.

an3.70.title: The Uposatha: Visākhā's Teaching
an3.70.setting: Sāvatthī, the Eastern Monastery, Migāramātā's mansion. Visākhā comes to the Buddha on an uposatha day.
an3.70.brief:
Three kinds of uposatha:
- the cowherd's: spent thinking about tomorrow's food
- the Jain's: precepts toward some beings but not others, and false renunciation
- **the noble one's**: the mind purified by recollecting the Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, one's own virtue and the deities, while keeping the eight precepts *"as the arahants do for life, so I for this day and night"*

The benefit of one such uposatha exceeds sovereignty over the sixteen great countries.
teaching: Five recollections purify the mind on uposatha: Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha, one's own virtue, the deities.
Each precept is undertaken by modelling the arahants: *yāvajīvaṃ arahanto … ahampajja imañca rattiṃ imañca divasaṃ…*
Rule over the sixteen great countries is "not worth a sixteenth part" of the noble uposatha.
an3.70.living: **This is the sutta behind the app's uposatha days.** Read it the evening before each observance. The five recollections can replace the usual evening sitting on uposatha days.

notes.text: "I, too, for this day and night…" The canonical source for observing uposatha from dawn to dawn, as The Path does.

an8.41.title: The Uposatha in Brief
an8.41.brief: The uposatha with eight factors. Each precept is taken with the same reflection: "For life, the arahants keep this. Today, for this day and night, I will keep it too." Observed like this, it is of great fruit.
teaching: Refraining from killing, stealing and all sexual activity.
Refraining from lying and from alcohol.
Refraining from eating after noon, from entertainment and adornment, and from high and luxurious beds.
"I will imitate the arahants for one day and night."

an8.42.title: The Uposatha in Detail
an8.42.brief: The same eight factors, then a measure of their worth. Rule over the sixteen great nations of India, with all their wealth, is not worth a sixteenth of the uposatha well kept. A day of the Four Great Kings' heaven is fifty human years; their life is five hundred of such years.
teaching: The eight factors, each in imitation of the arahants.
Human kingship is "poor beside divine happiness".
The lifespans of the six sense-sphere heavens, as the measure of the fruit.

an8.43.title: Visākhā's Uposatha
an8.43.setting: Sāvatthī, the Eastern Monastery. Taught to the laywoman Visākhā.
an8.43.brief: The uposatha with eight factors explained to Visākhā, the greatest laywoman supporter, with its fruit measured against human sovereignty and the heavens.
teaching: The eight factors.
Their fruit beside kingship and divine life.
Verses: women and men who keep it are reborn in heaven.

an9.18.title: The Uposatha with Nine Factors
an9.18.brief: The eight precepts with a ninth factor: **dwelling with a heart of loving-kindness** that spreads in every direction, above, below and across, abundant and boundless. This is the canonical basis of the nine-precept observance (*navaṅga sīla*).
teaching: The eight uposatha precepts.
The ninth: mettā pervading the whole world.
Great fruit, great glory, great radiance.

an5.198.title: Well-Spoken Words
an5.198.brief: Speech with five factors is well spoken, blameless and not faulted by the wise: it is spoken **at the right time**, it is **true**, it is **gentle**, it is **beneficial**, and it is spoken **with a mind of love**.
teaching: At the right time (*kāla*).
True (*sacca*).
Gentle (*saṇha*).
Beneficial (*atthasaṃhita*).
With a loving mind (*mettacitta*).
an5.198.living: Before an email or a difficult conversation, run the five checks. Most regretted words fail on timing or on the last one, the state of heart they were spoken from.

mn58.title: Prince Abhaya
mn58.setting: Rājagaha. The Jain leader sends Prince Abhaya with a trick question meant to corner the Buddha: would you ever say something that hurts another?
mn58.brief: Prince Abhaya has his baby son on his lap. The Buddha answers with an example from his own home: if the child put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, you would remove it even if it drew blood, out of compassion. Then he gives the most precise teaching on speech in the canon: whether to speak depends on three things — is it true, is it beneficial, is it welcome — and also on the right time.
teaching: Untrue, harmful, unwelcome: he does not say it.
True but harmful: he does not say it.
True, beneficial but unwelcome: he knows the right time to say it.
True, beneficial and welcome: he knows the right time to say it.
All of it from compassion for beings.

an4.100.title: Potaliya
an4.100.setting: Sāvatthī. The wanderer Potaliya thinks the best person is the one who neither praises nor criticises.
an4.100.brief: Four kinds of people: those who criticise the blameworthy truly and at the right time but do not praise; those who praise but do not criticise; those who do neither; and those who do both, truly and at the right time. The Buddha says the last is best: "knowing the right time" is the excellent thing.
teaching: Equanimity that never praises or corrects is not the highest.
The best person speaks both praise and criticism, truthfully and at the right time.

an4.183.title: What Has Been Heard
an4.183.setting: Rājagaha. The chief minister Vassakāra claims there is no fault in speaking of whatever one has seen, heard, sensed or known.
an4.183.brief: The Buddha disagrees. Not everything seen, heard, sensed or known should be spoken. The test is the effect: if saying it makes unwholesome qualities grow and wholesome ones decline, it should not be said; if the reverse, it should.
teaching: Truth alone is not the test for speech.
Ask what the words will cause to grow, in yourself and in others.

an10.176.title: Cunda the Smith
an10.176.setting: Pāvā, Cunda's mango grove. Cunda describes the purification rites of the western brahmins: touching earth and cow dung, bathing three times, tending fire.
an10.176.brief: The Buddha replaces ritual purity with ethical purity. There are three kinds of impurity of body, four of speech and three of mind: the ten unwholesome courses of action. Someone who does them is impure whether or not they touch the earth at dawn; someone who refrains is pure.
teaching: **Body:** killing, stealing, sexual misconduct.
**Speech:** lying, divisive, harsh and idle speech.
**Mind:** covetousness, ill will, wrong view.
Purity is these ten given up, not a rite performed.

an5.161.title: Removing Resentment
an5.161.brief: Five ways to remove resentment toward a person, whatever it has grown from: develop **loving-kindness** for them; develop **compassion**; develop **equanimity**; **stop paying attention** to them; and reflect that they are **the owner of their own deeds**.
teaching: Mettā toward that person.
Compassion toward that person.
Equanimity toward that person.
Disregard: do not keep turning the mind to them.
Kamma: "This person owns their deeds and will inherit them."
an5.161.living: A toolkit in order of gentleness. When love will not come, try compassion; when compassion will not come, equanimity; when none will come, simply stop feeding the thought; and finally hand the matter over to kamma.

an7.64.title: An Angry Person
an7.64.brief: Seven things an enemy wishes on you, which an angry person does to themselves: to be ugly, to sleep badly, to fail to prosper, to lose wealth, to lose reputation, to lose friends, and to be reborn in a bad place. The long verses describe anger as it really is: it blinds, it wounds the family, it can even drive a person to self-harm, and it is the root of much regret.
teaching: Anger fulfils the enemy's seven wishes.
"An angry person does not know what is good."
Self-control, wisdom, energy and right view burn anger out like a fire out of fuel.

sn7.2.title: Abuse
sn7.2.setting: Rājagaha. The brahmin Akkosaka Bhāradvāja, furious that his clansman has become a monk, insults the Buddha to his face.
sn7.2.brief: The Buddha asks him: when guests do not accept the food you offer, whose is it? "Mine." So too: "I do not accept your abuse. It is yours, brahmin." The verses that follow are a classic on patience.
teaching: Abuse not accepted stays with the one who gave it.
Repaying anger with anger is worse; not repaying it wins a battle hard to win.
Staying calm when another is angry heals both: oneself and the other.

mn21.title: The Simile of the Saw
mn21.setting: Sāvatthī. Venerable Moḷiyaphagguna mixes too closely with the nuns and flares up when they are criticised.
mn21.brief: One of the great teachings on patience. People will speak to you in five ways: timely or untimely, true or false, gentle or harsh, beneficial or harmful, with love or with hate. In every case: "Our minds will be unaffected; we will dwell with a heart of love." Even if bandits sawed you limb from limb, one who gave way to hate would not be following the teaching.
teaching: The housewife Vedehikā was known as gentle until her maid tested her by sleeping in: gentleness is proven only when tested.
The five ways others may speak to us.
Similes: the earth that cannot be dug away, space that cannot be painted, the Ganges that cannot be heated with a grass torch, the soft catskin bag that does not rustle.
The saw: even then, mettā.

an4.256.title: Four Ways of Holding People Together
an4.256.brief:
Four bases of sympathy, by which a leader, a family head or anyone holds others together:
- giving (dāna)
- kindly speech (peyyavajja)
- beneficial conduct (atthacariyā)
- impartiality (samānattatā)
teaching: These four reappear at the close of DN 31 as "the linchpin of the world".
an4.256.living: **The Buddhist theory of leadership in four words.** Every relationship of authority (employer, parent, ruler) is held together by these. Sri Lankan royal inscriptions and chronicles invoke them as marks of a righteous king.

notes.text: Sujato: "equality". The commentary reads it as treating others as oneself and sharing their joys and sorrows. In leadership terms: being the same person to everyone, without favouritism.

dn16x.title: The Seven Conditions of Non-Decline · Virtue and Its Fruits
dn16x.known: from the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta (DN 16) · මහාපරිනිබ්බාන සූත්‍රය
dn16x.setting: Vulture's Peak, Rājagaha. King Ajātasattu of Magadha plans to destroy the Vajjian republic and sends his chief minister Vassakāra to learn what the Buddha will say. Later, at Pāṭali Village, the Buddha teaches the local lay followers and foresees the great city Pāṭaliputta being built.
dn16x.brief:
Two excerpts from the long account of the Buddha's last journey.

**First, the seven conditions under which a people will grow and not decline:**
1. meeting often and in large numbers
2. meeting, rising and acting in harmony
3. not making new laws or abolishing old ones, but following the ancient constitution
4. honouring and heeding elders
5. not abducting or coercing women and girls
6. honouring and maintaining shrines and offerings
7. protecting holy people

**Second, at Pāṭali Village**, the five dangers of immorality and the five benefits of virtue for a householder. The first benefit is great wealth through heedfulness; the first danger is great loss through heedlessness.
teaching: As long as the Vajjis keep these seven, "growth is to be expected, not decline". Vassakāra concludes that Magadha cannot defeat them by war, only by diplomacy or by sowing division.
The immoral person loses wealth through heedlessness, gains a bad name, is uneasy in any assembly, dies confused and is reborn badly.
The virtuous person gains great wealth through heedfulness, a good name, confidence in any assembly, an unconfused death and a good rebirth.
Pāṭaliputta is founded as a bulwark against the Vajjis. The Buddha foretells its greatness and its three dangers: fire, flood and internal dissension.
dn16x.living:
**Seven conditions for any institution.** Swap "Vajjis" for a family, a company or a board. Meet often. Decide together. Respect established rules. Honour elders. Protect the vulnerable. Maintain what is sacred. Protect good people. The minister's conclusion is the sharpest line: such a body can be beaten only by division from within.

**The five benefits of virtue are the summary of Part II:** *wealth through heedfulness* is the first fruit of keeping precepts.

notes.text: "Have many meetings." The first condition of a republic's strength is frequent, well-attended assembly. Sujato's rendering is accurate.

dn26.title: The Wheel-Turning Monarch
dn26.setting: Mātulā in Magadha. The Buddha tells the monks to be islands unto themselves and keep to their own ancestral pastures, the four foundations of mindfulness. Then he tells a story of kings.
dn26.brief:
King Daḷhanemi, a wheel-turning monarch, hands the realm to his son with the noble duty of a sovereign:
- rely on Dhamma, honour it, make it your banner
- provide just protection for all: household, army, nobles, brahmins and householders, town and country, renunciants, beasts and birds
- **let no wrongdoing prevail in the realm**
- **give wealth to those without it**
- consult renunciants about what is wholesome

Generations later a king provides protection but **does not give wealth to the poor**. Poverty spreads, then theft. The king first gives a thief money, which only spreads theft. Then he executes thieves, which brings weapons. Weapons bring killing, then lying, slander, sexual misconduct and every vice, until human lifespan falls to ten years and a "sword interval" of mutual slaughter comes. The survivors turn back to goodness, and life and prosperity grow again. The sutta closes with the future Buddha Metteyya.
teaching: The duty of a righteous ruler includes **giving wealth to the destitute** (*adhanānaṃ dhanamanuppadāna*).
Neglecting the poor is the first link in the chain of social collapse: poverty, theft, weapons, killing, lies.
Punishment alone does not cure crime born of poverty. It escalates violence.
Social restoration begins with individuals choosing goodness.
The frame: for a monk, the ancestral domain is mindfulness. "Keep to your own pastures."
dn26.living:
**The canonical theory of why crime happens.** Not original sin, not bad blood: *poverty unattended by the state*. The king who failed did everything else right. He kept just protection. He failed only at one duty, giving to the destitute, and the whole society unravelled.

**Read with DN 5.** DN 5 is the positive programme (seed, capital, wages). DN 26 is what happens when it is neglected.

**For a private person of means,** the analogue is the duty in AN 4.61 and DN 31 to support those who depend on you. Your household is a small realm.

notes.text: "Provide money to the penniless in the realm." Literal and accurate.
"From not providing money to the penniless, poverty became widespread…" The causal chain is explicit in the Pali, and Sujato preserves it faithfully.

dn5.title: Kūṭadanta: The Sacrifice Without Killing
dn5.setting: Khāṇumata, a brahmin village of Magadha. The wealthy brahmin Kūṭadanta has prepared a great sacrifice: seven hundred bulls, bullocks, heifers, goats and rams tied to the posts. He comes to ask the Buddha how to perform it.
dn5.brief:
The Buddha tells of King Mahāvijita, who wished to make a great sacrifice. His chaplain first advised him on the state of the country. The land is beset by bandits, and taxing it now would be wrong. Punishing the bandits by execution, prison and fines would not end the problem. Instead the king should:
- give **seed and food** to those who farm and keep cattle
- give **capital** to those in trade
- give **food and wages** to those in government service

The people, busy with their work, will not harass the country, revenues will grow, and the land will be at peace, *"people dancing with children at their breast, living with doors unbarred"*.

Then the sacrifice itself, made with the consent of four constituencies (nobles, ministers, brahmins and householders), used only ghee, oil, butter, curd, honey and molasses. No animals were killed, no trees felled, no labourers coerced. Higher still are perpetual giving, building dwellings for the Sangha, going for refuge, the precepts, and finally the path to liberation. Kūṭadanta frees all the animals.
teaching: Do not raise taxes on a country already suffering (*balimuddhareyya, akiccakārī assa*).
Crime is not ended by punishment alone but by livelihood.
Economic policy: seed and food for farmers, capital for merchants, fair wages for officials.
Consult the four constituencies before a great undertaking.
The greatest sacrifice is no sacrifice of life at all, culminating in liberation.
dn5.living:
**The oldest stimulus programme on record.** Seed and food for the productive base, working capital for commerce, fair pay for the civil service. Result: crime falls, revenue rises, and "people live with their doors open". All of it happens before the sacrifice, as its precondition.

**On tax:** the first counsel is *restraint*. A ruler who taxes a suffering country "would not be doing his duty". The same text is the canonical warrant for reading *bali* as tax and for the principle that its burden must be just.

**On large undertakings:** before acting, the king consults four constituencies and gains their consent. That is a practice for any household or institution about to commit great resources.

notes.text: Sujato: "seed and fodder". *Bhatta* is food or rations, not fodder. The Buddha Jayanti Sinhala has **බිජු ද බත් ද**, "seed and rice". The king feeds the farmers through the season and gives them seed to plant.
"Funding": the Buddha Jayanti Sinhala has **බඩුමිල**, money for goods. This is working capital for traders. Accurate.
"If the king were to extract more taxes while his realm is thus harried… he would not be doing his duty." *Bali* here is plainly tax, which supports reading *rājabali* in AN 4.61 the same way.

dn27.title: The Origin of Things: The First King
dn27.setting: Sāvatthī, the Eastern Monastery. Two brahmin novices, Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja, tell the Buddha that their fellow brahmins abuse them for leaving the "highest caste".
dn27.brief:
The Buddha tells a story of origins. As beings grew greedy, food coarsened, private property appeared, and with it theft, lies and punishment. The people gathered and chose the most handsome, gracious and capable among them to censure, rebuke and banish rightly, paying him a share of rice. He was called:
- **Mahāsammata**, "approved by the great people"
- **Khattiya**, "lord of the fields"
- **Rājā**, "one who delights others by Dhamma"

Caste is shown to be a social arrangement, not divine. The conclusion: *"Dhamma is the best thing for people, in this life and the next."*
teaching: Kingship arose by social agreement, to keep order, and was paid for by the people.
A king is called *rājā* because he delights others by Dhamma (*dhammena pare rañjeti*).
All four classes are equal in moral consequence. Conduct, not birth, determines worth.
*Dhammo hi seṭṭho janetasmiṃ*: Dhamma is supreme among people.
dn27.living:
**Kingship as a contract.** The first ruler was chosen for capacity and paid to keep order. His title meant one who *delights* the people through Dhamma. Authority is legitimate when it does that job and loses its meaning when it doesn't.

**For anyone proud of lineage,** the sutta's teaching is pointed. Kingship begins with an agreement to rule righteously, and "conduct, not birth" is its final word.

notes.text: Sujato: "popularly elected". The Pali is "agreed upon by the great multitude". "Elected" carries modern ballot-box connotations. The traditional English is "the Great Elect" or "the Great Appointee". The Buddha Jayanti Sinhala uses *sammata kara gannemu*, "let us agree upon one". The Sinhala chronicles trace the island's royal lines back to Mahāsammata.

an4.70.title: Unrighteous Rulers
an4.70.brief:
When kings are unrighteous, their officials become unrighteous. Then the brahmins and householders, then the people of town and country. Then sun and moon go awry, the seasons, the winds and the rains, crops ripen unevenly, and people become short-lived and sickly. When kings are righteous, the reverse.

The verse: when cattle cross a river, if the lead bull goes crooked, all go crooked. If he goes straight, all go straight.
teaching: Righteousness and its absence flow downward from the top.
The herd follows the lead bull.
an4.70.living: **Tone at the top, in its oldest form.** Whatever you lead (a household, a company, a team), people take their standard from you. The verse is worth keeping in view: the herd follows the bull.

notes.text: "If the bull goes off course." The verse's image of a herd crossing a river is the canon's clearest statement of leadership by example.

an5.133.title: The King of the King
an5.133.brief: Even a righteous wheel-turning monarch does not rule without a king of his own. Who is it? **The Dhamma.** He relies on Dhamma, honours it, takes it as his banner, his flag and his authority, and provides just protection for every class, down to beasts and birds. In the same way the Buddha, the king of Dhamma, provides protection for monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.
teaching: No legitimate power is sovereign over itself. The ruler's ruler is the Dhamma.
an5.133.living: **Above every authority stands Dhamma.** For anyone holding power over others: you are not the final authority in your own domain. Decide as one who answers to something higher.

notes.text: "Does not wield power without having their own king." Accurate. The wheel is never turned "kingless".

sn3.13.title: A Bucket of Rice: The King Who Ate Too Much
sn3.13.setting: Sāvatthī. King Pasenadi, having eaten a whole bucket-measure of rice and curry, comes to the Buddha huffing and puffing.
sn3.13.brief: The Buddha recites a verse: a mindful person who knows moderation in food has fewer ailments, ages slowly and guards his life. Pasenadi has a young man, Sudassana, learn it and recite it at every meal for a hundred coins a day. The king gradually reduces to a cup of rice, becomes slim, and stroking his limbs declares that the Buddha has done him good in two ways, for this life and the next.
teaching: Moderation in eating is mindfulness in practice and protection of life.
sn3.13.living: **A king's health is a state matter.** The Buddha does not lecture. He gives a verse, and the king designs his own reminder system: a paid reciter at every meal. A model for building any new habit.

notes.text: "A person who's always mindful… knows moderation in food". Accurate.

sn3.17.title: Heedfulness: The Elephant's Footprint
sn3.17.setting: Sāvatthī. King Pasenadi asks whether there is one thing that secures both kinds of welfare, in this life and the next.
sn3.17.brief: There is: heedfulness (*appamāda*). As the footprints of all animals fit inside the elephant's, all good qualities fit inside heedfulness. The verse: one who desires long life, health, beauty, heaven and high birth should praise heedfulness in making merit.
teaching: Heedfulness is the one quality that secures welfare here and hereafter.
sn3.17.living: **One word to carry.** When everything else is too much to remember, the Buddha gives the king one word. Every quality in this library fits inside its footprint.

notes.text: "Diligence" or "heedfulness". Sujato uses "diligence". The sense is vigilance, never letting the wholesome lapse.

sn3.25.title: The Simile of the Mountains
sn3.25.setting: Sāvatthī. King Pasenadi arrives at midday, absorbed in the business of kingship.
sn3.25.brief: The Buddha asks: suppose trusted men came from the four directions, each saying "a great mountain as high as the sky is coming this way, crushing every living thing". With such peril at hand and human life so hard to come by, what should be done? Pasenadi: "What else but to live righteously, act well, and make merit?" The Buddha: old age and death are rolling toward you. Pasenadi admits that elephants, cavalry, chariots, infantry, counsel and treasure are all useless against them.
teaching: Against ageing and death, armies, diplomacy and treasure have no power. Only Dhamma and merit do.
sn3.25.living: **Written for the powerful.** The king's own admission (his armies, his counsellors, his treasury, all useless here) is what makes this sutta work. Read it on the busiest day of the year. The verse ends: *"So the wise person, seeing his own good, should establish faith in the Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha."*

notes.text: "Old age and death are advancing on you." Sujato's rendering is accurate. The mountains are the four directions closing in.

ja534.title: The Ten Royal Virtues
ja534.known: Dasa Rājadhamma · from the Mahāhaṃsa Jātaka (Jā 534) · දශරාජ ධර්මය
ja534.setting: A Jātaka. The swan-king Dhataraṭṭha, captured and brought before the king of Benares, asks after his welfare. In answer the king names the ten qualities he stands in.
ja534.brief:
The ten virtues of a righteous king, which the Sinhala tradition treats as the constitution of kingship:
1. giving (dāna)
2. virtue (sīla)
3. liberality (pariccāga)
4. honesty (ajjava)
5. gentleness (maddava)
6. austerity (tapa)
7. non-anger (akkodha)
8. non-violence (avihiṃsā)
9. patience (khanti)
10. non-opposition (avirodhana)
teaching: "Standing in these ten, I do not fear the next world. Seeing these wholesome qualities in myself, great joy and gladness arise in me."
ja534.living: **The Sri Lankan ideal of the ruler.** Chronicles, inscriptions and sermons hold kings to these ten. They are equally a standard for anyone who leads, whether a household, a company or a community.

notes.text: These verses have no Sujato translation; the English here is mine, checked against the Buddha Jayanti Sinhala. That Sinhala glosses *tapa* as keeping the uposatha precepts (උපෝසථශීලසමාදාන), *akkodha* as non-anger rooted in mettā, *avihiṃsā* as non-violence rooted in karuṇā, *khanti* as forbearance, and *avirodhana* as being in accord (එකඟබව), not opposing what is right.

sn3.1.title: Young
sn3.1.setting: Sāvatthī. King Pasenadi of Kosala meets the Buddha for the first time.
sn3.1.brief: The king doubts that someone so young can claim full awakening when older teachers do not. The Buddha names four things not to be looked down on because they are young: **a prince, a snake, a fire and a mendicant**. Pasenadi goes for refuge.
teaching: A young prince may become king and take revenge.
A small snake can kill.
A small fire can burn a forest.
A young mendicant may be fully awakened.

sn3.2.title: A Person
sn3.2.brief: What arises within a person to their harm? **Greed, hatred and delusion**. They destroy the one in whom they arise, as a reed is destroyed by its own fruit.
teaching: The three roots of the unwholesome.
They harm the very one who harbours them.

sn3.3.title: Old Age and Death
sn3.3.brief: Is anyone born free of old age and death? No one: not the wealthy, not the learned, not even the arahants, whose bodies break up too. Royal chariots wear out, but the Dhamma of the good does not grow old.
teaching: No one born is free of ageing and death.
"The Dhamma of the good does not decay."

sn3.4.title: Dear
sn3.4.setting: Sāvatthī. The king reports a reflection from his own retreat.
sn3.4.brief: Those who do wrong in body, speech and mind treat themselves as an enemy would, even if they say "I love myself". Those who do good love themselves, even if they say they do not.
teaching: Self-love is shown by conduct, not by words.
Good deeds are the real kindness to oneself.

sn3.5.title: Self-Protected
sn3.5.brief: A wrongdoer surrounded by elephants, cavalry, chariots and infantry is still unprotected, because the protection is outside. Someone of good conduct with no army is protected, because the protection is within.
teaching: Real protection is internal: restraint of body, speech and mind.

sn3.6.title: Few
sn3.6.brief: Few in the world, having gained great wealth, are not intoxicated by it, careless, greedy for pleasures and unjust to others. Many are. Like deer falling into a trap they do not see.
teaching: Wealth tests character.
The rich who stay sober and fair are rare.

sn3.7.title: In the Court
sn3.7.setting: Sāvatthī. The king, sitting in judgement.
sn3.7.brief: Pasenadi tells the Buddha he has had enough of judging cases: he sees wealthy nobles, brahmins and householders lying knowingly for the sake of pleasure and gain. The Buddha agrees that this leads to long harm.
teaching: Justice is corrupted by greed at every level of society.
The king's weariness is itself a moral observation.

sn3.8.title: Mallikā
sn3.8.setting: Sāvatthī. In the palace, the king asks Queen Mallikā whether anyone is dearer to her than herself.
sn3.8.brief: Mallikā answers honestly: no one, and asks him the same. He agrees. The Buddha confirms it: search every direction and you will find no one dearer than yourself. And since others too love themselves, one who loves himself should not harm another.
teaching: No one is dearer than oneself.
Others feel the same about themselves.
Therefore do not harm others: the Golden Rule grounded in honest self-knowledge.

sn3.9.title: Sacrifice
sn3.9.setting: Sāvatthī. A great animal sacrifice is being prepared for the king; the servants weep as they work.
sn3.9.brief: The Buddha says the great Vedic sacrifices of horse and man do not bear great fruit. Sacrifices without slaughter, offered regularly to the virtuous, do.
teaching: Sacrifice that requires killing is not of great fruit.
Bloodless offerings to the good are.

sn3.10.title: Bonds
sn3.10.setting: Sāvatthī. The king has many people put in chains.
sn3.10.brief: The wise do not call iron, wood or rope a strong bond. Infatuation with jewels, children and partners is the strong bond. It holds us down, and it is hard to escape.
teaching: Attachment is the real prison.

sn3.11.title: Seven Matted-Hair Ascetics
sn3.11.setting: Sāvatthī, the Eastern Monastery. The king pays homage to a group of passing ascetics.
sn3.11.brief: It is hard for a householder to know who is an arahant. **Virtue is known by living with someone, integrity by dealing with them, resilience in adversity, wisdom in discussion**, and only over a long time, by one who is attentive and wise. Pasenadi then admits the ascetics were his own spies.
teaching: Four ways to know a person: living together, dealing together, adversity, discussion.
Over a long time, with attention and wisdom.
Do not judge by appearance.
sn3.11.living: Perhaps the best due-diligence advice in the canon. Character shows in shared life, in business dealings, under pressure and in conversation, and it takes time to see.

sn3.12.title: Five Kings
sn3.12.setting: Sāvatthī. Five kings, Pasenadi among them, debate which of the senses gives the highest pleasure.
sn3.12.brief: The Buddha says the highest pleasure is whatever is most agreeable to each person: preference, not the object, sets the limit. The lay follower Candanaṅgalika then praises the Buddha in verse, and the five kings give him five robes.
teaching: The "best" pleasure is subjective.

sn3.14.title: The Battle (1)
sn3.14.setting: Kosala. Pasenadi is defeated in battle by his nephew Ajātasattu of Magadha.
sn3.14.brief: The Buddha's verse on war: **victory breeds enmity; the defeated sleep in pain. The peaceful sleep at ease, having given up victory and defeat.**
teaching: Victory begets hatred; defeat begets suffering.
Peace is beyond both.

sn3.15.title: The Battle (2)
sn3.15.setting: Kosala. In a later battle Pasenadi wins and captures Ajātasattu alive.
sn3.15.brief: He confiscates the army but spares his nephew. The Buddha comments: a man plunders while it suits him, then others plunder him. **The killer gets a killer, the conqueror a conqueror**; by the turning of deeds, the plunderer is plundered.
teaching: Mercy in victory.
Violence returns: "by the evolution of deeds."

sn3.16.title: A Daughter
sn3.16.setting: Sāvatthī. News arrives that Queen Mallikā has given birth to a daughter, and the king is displeased.
sn3.16.brief: The Buddha corrects him: **a daughter may turn out better than a son**: wise, virtuous, respectful to her husband's family and devoted. The son she bears may become a hero and a ruler.
teaching: A daughter is not a lesser birth.
Wisdom and virtue, not gender, decide worth.

sn3.18.title: Good Friends
sn3.18.brief: Pasenadi reflects that the Dhamma is for one with good friends. The Buddha recalls telling Ānanda that good friendship is **the whole of the spiritual life**. He tells the king to rely on diligence (*appamāda*): then his queens, his court, his army and the people will be diligent too, and his treasury will be protected.
teaching: "Good friendship is the whole of the holy life."
A diligent ruler makes a diligent people.

sn3.21.title: Persons
sn3.21.brief: Four kinds of people: from **dark to dark**, **dark to light**, **light to dark** and **light to light**. Birth into hardship or privilege is not destiny; conduct decides where one goes.
teaching: Born low, living badly: dark to dark.
Born low, living well: dark to light.
Born high, living badly: light to dark.
Born high, living well: light to light.

sn3.22.title: Grandmother
sn3.22.setting: Sāvatthī. The king comes in the middle of the day: his grandmother has died at the age of one hundred and twenty.
sn3.22.brief: He would have given an elephant, a horse, a village, even the country, to keep her alive. The Buddha: all beings die, like a potter's vessels, baked or unbaked. The good one has done is a support in the next world.
teaching: All beings end in death.
Merit is the support beyond this life.

sn3.23.title: The World
sn3.23.brief: Three things arise in the world for harm, suffering and discomfort: **greed, hatred and delusion**.
teaching: The three roots again, as the source of the world's troubles.

sn3.24.title: Archery
sn3.24.setting: Sāvatthī. The king asks where a gift should be given.
sn3.24.brief: Two different questions, the Buddha says. **Where should one give?** Wherever the heart has confidence. **Where is a gift most fruitful?** In the virtuous, free of the five hindrances. As a king hires an archer for skill, not for caste, so the worth of a recipient lies in their qualities, not their birth.
teaching: Give where the heart is inspired.
Great fruit comes from giving to the virtuous.
Merit, not birth: the archer simile.

dn2.title: The Fruits of the Contemplative Life
dn2.setting: Rājagaha, a full-moon night in Kattika. King Ajātasattu, who had his father killed, cannot rest and asks to visit a teacher.
dn2.brief: He has asked six famous teachers what visible fruit the contemplative life brings, and found their answers empty. The Buddha begins simply: even a servant or a farmer who goes forth is honoured by the king himself. Then he lays out the whole path, fruit by fruit: virtue, sense restraint, contentment, abandoning the hindrances, the four jhānas with their similes, and the knowledges up to liberation. The king confesses his crime.
teaching: A complete map of the gradual path.
The hindrances as debt, illness, prison, slavery and a desert crossing.
The jhāna similes: bath powder kneaded with water, a lake fed from within, lotuses immersed, a man wrapped in white cloth.
The Buddha later says that had the king not killed his father, the eye of the Dhamma would have opened in him then.

dn17.title: King Mahāsudassana
dn17.setting: Kusinārā, as the Buddha lies on his final bed. Ānanda wishes he would not pass away in such a small town.
dn17.brief: The Buddha tells him that Kusinārā was once the royal city Kusāvatī, capital of the great king Mahāsudassana. He had seven treasures, four kinds of success and a palace of the Dhamma, yet he withdrew to practise the jhānas and the divine abodes. All of it has vanished: "How impermanent are conditions."
teaching: The ideal king: generous, righteous, beloved.
Even perfect worldly success is let go.
*Aniccā vata saṅkhārā*: the verse chanted at Sri Lankan funerals.

mn82.title: Raṭṭhapāla
mn82.setting: Thullakoṭṭhita, Kuru country. A wealthy young man fasts until his parents allow him to go forth. Years later, as an arahant, he visits home and declines his inheritance.
mn82.brief: King Koravya asks why he went forth, since he had suffered none of the four losses (old age, illness, wealth, relatives). Raṭṭhapāla answers with **four summaries of the Dhamma**, each proven by questioning the king about his own life.
teaching: **The world is unstable; it is swept away.**
**The world has no shelter and no protector.**
**The world owns nothing; one must go on leaving everything.**
**The world is wanting, insatiable, the slave of craving.**

mn83.title: King Maghadeva
mn83.setting: Mithilā, Maghadeva's mango grove. The Buddha smiles at a certain spot and tells its story.
mn83.brief: A dynasty of righteous kings, each of whom, on finding his first grey hair, crowned his son and went forth. The custom held for generations, until a king broke it. That good custom led to the Brahmā realm; the Buddha's good custom, the eightfold path, leads to nibbāna. "Don't be the last man to keep it."
teaching: The grey hair as a divine messenger.
Righteous succession: hand on the kingdom while still well.
Do not be the one who breaks a good tradition.

mn89.title: Monuments to the Dhamma
mn89.setting: Medaḷumpa, among the Sakyans. The aged King Pasenadi visits the Buddha, kisses his feet, and declares his love.
mn89.brief: Asked why, the king gives ten reasons for his faith, which the Buddha calls **monuments to the Dhamma**: monks who live in harmony like milk and water, while kings, brahmins and families quarrel; disciples who stay devoted for life; even his own ministers who prefer the Buddha's teaching to the king's favour. Meanwhile his general has taken the royal regalia; the king will soon die in exile.
teaching: The Saṅgha's harmony as evidence of the Teaching.
Faith grounded in what one has seen.
The poignancy of a king at the end of power.

mn90.title: At Kaṇṇakatthala
mn90.setting: Ujuññā, the deer park at Kaṇṇakatthala. King Pasenadi questions the Buddha.
mn90.brief: The king asks about omniscience, the four castes, the gods and Brahmā. On caste, the Buddha says that among those who strive in the five factors (faith, health, honesty, energy, wisdom), there is no difference in the freedom gained, as fires of different woods give the same flame.
teaching: No one knows and sees everything at once.
Striving, not birth, determines liberation.

mn86.title: Aṅgulimāla
mn86.setting: Sāvatthī and the Kosalan forest. The Buddha walks into the territory of the killer who wears a garland of fingers.
mn86.brief: "Stop, ascetic!" — "I have stopped, Aṅgulimāla; you stop too." The killer becomes a monk. King Pasenadi arrives with an army to capture him and finds a mendicant. The sutta contains the **Aṅgulimāla paritta**, chanted for women in labour, and the verse: one who covers bad deeds with good lights up the world like the moon freed from cloud.
teaching: No one is beyond redemption.
The king who comes with soldiers is shown peace that force could not achieve.
The paritta: "Since my noble birth, I do not recall intentionally taking life. By this truth, may you be well, and your child."

mn108.title: Gopaka Moggallāna
mn108.setting: Rājagaha, soon after the Buddha's death. The city is being fortified against King Pajjota; the chief minister Vassakāra questions Ānanda.
mn108.brief: Is there a single monk the Buddha appointed as successor, or whom the Saṅgha has chosen? No. Then how does the Saṅgha stay united? "We are not without refuge; **the Dhamma is our refuge**." Ānanda describes the ten qualities that make a monk worthy of respect, and the institution that works by principle rather than by a leader.
teaching: No successor: the Dhamma and the training rules govern.
Ten qualities that inspire confidence.
Institutional continuity without a single head.

an7.21.title: At Sārandada
an7.21.setting: Vesālī, the Sārandada shrine. The Licchavis come to the Buddha.
an7.21.brief: Seven principles of non-decline for a republic: **meet often and in full; meet, act and disperse in harmony; do not legislate arbitrarily, keep the established law; honour the elders; do not abduct women and girls; maintain the shrines and their offerings; protect the arahants.** As long as they keep these, only growth is to be expected.
teaching: Frequent, full assemblies.
Concord in meeting and acting.
Rule of law, not of whim.
Respect for elders.
Protection of women.
Care of sacred places.
Protection of the holy.

an7.22.title: Vassakāra
an7.22.setting: Rājagaha, Vulture's Peak. King Ajātasattu wants to destroy the Vajjians and sends his chief minister to sound out the Buddha.
an7.22.brief: The Buddha asks Ānanda whether the Vajjians still keep the seven principles. They do. Vassakāra draws the conclusion: they cannot be defeated in war, except by bribery or by breaking their unity. Then the Buddha applies the same principles to the Saṅgha.
teaching: A united, lawful people is not conquered by force.
Their weak points are corruption and division.

an4.187.title: Vassakāra on Judging People
an4.187.setting: Rājagaha. Vassakāra asks whether a bad person can recognise a good one.
an4.187.brief: A bad person cannot know a bad person, nor a good one. A good person can know both. It takes goodness to judge character.
teaching: Only the good can judge goodness, and badness, accurately.

an5.49.title: Kosala
an5.49.setting: Sāvatthī. As King Pasenadi sits with the Buddha, a man whispers in his ear that Queen Mallikā has died.
an5.49.brief: The king sits slumped, shoulders drooping, lost for words. The Buddha teaches the **five things no one can obtain**: that what is subject to ageing should not age, sickness not sicken, death not die, ending not end, perishing not perish.
teaching: Five things unobtainable by anyone in the world.
The wise, reflecting, do not sorrow; the arrow is pulled out.

an5.50.title: Nārada
an5.50.setting: Pāṭaliputta. King Muṇḍa's beloved Queen Bhaddā has died; he will not bathe or eat, neglects the kingdom, and broods over her body.
an5.50.brief: His treasurer takes him to Venerable Nārada, who teaches the five unobtainable things and the verses on grief. The king puts down his sorrow, has the body cremated, builds a memorial, and returns to his duties. BJT names it "the removing of the dart of sorrow".
teaching: Grief does not bring back the dead, and it delights one's enemies.
The arrow of sorrow can be drawn out.

sn55.1.title: A Wheel-Turning King
sn55.1.brief: A wheel-turning monarch rules the four continents and is reborn in heaven, yet without four qualities he is not free from the lower realms. A noble disciple who lives on scraps and wears rags, but has **confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, and the virtue dear to the noble ones**, is free of them. The four continents are not worth a sixteenth of these four.
teaching: The four factors of stream-entry.
World empire is worth less than inner assurance.

an8.25.title: Who Is a Lay Follower?
an8.25.setting: Kapilavatthu, the Banyan Monastery. The Buddha's cousin Mahānāma asks.
an8.25.brief: One who has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha is a lay follower. A **virtuous** lay follower keeps the five precepts. A lay follower practising **for their own good** has faith, virtue and generosity, likes to see monastics, listens, remembers, examines the meaning and practises accordingly. One practising **for the good of both** also encourages others in each of these.
teaching: Refuge makes a lay follower.
The five precepts make a virtuous one.
Eight qualities for one's own good.
Encouraging others in them: for the good of both.

an5.175.title: The Outcaste Lay Follower
an5.175.brief: A lay follower with five qualities is an "outcaste", a stain: **faithless, unvirtuous, superstitious** (relying on omens and lucky signs rather than deeds), **seeking recipients outside the Dispensation**, and **serving them first**. One with the opposite five is a jewel, a lotus.
teaching: Outcaste by conduct, not birth.
Superstition (*kotūhalamaṅgala*): trusting omens over kamma.
The jewel lay follower trusts deeds, not signs.
an5.175.living: A gentle but firm word against horoscope-driven life. The Buddha does not mock the search for good fortune; he points to its real source, which is conduct.

an5.179.title: The Householder
an5.179.setting: Sāvatthī. Anāthapiṇḍika comes with five hundred lay followers; the Buddha addresses Sāriputta.
an5.179.brief: A lay person who is restrained in the five precepts and gains, whenever they wish, **four pleasant abidings in this very life** (confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the virtue dear to the noble ones) may declare: I am a stream-enterer, no longer bound for the lower realms.
teaching: Stream-entry is open to householders.
Five precepts plus four kinds of confidence.
The four "heavenly abidings of the higher mind" (*ābhicetasika diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).

sn55.7.title: The People of Bamboo Gate
sn55.7.setting: The Kosalan village of Veḷudvāra. The brahmin householders ask: we want family, fine clothes, perfumes and money, and a good rebirth. Teach us accordingly.
sn55.7.brief: The Buddha teaches the **Golden Rule** in its fullest canonical form. "I want to live and don't want to die; I want happiness and dislike pain. If someone took my life, I would not like it. Others feel the same. How could I do to another what I would not want done to me?" Applied to killing, stealing, adultery, lying, divisive, harsh and idle speech. With the four factors of stream-entry, it leads to the stream.
teaching: Reflect on yourself, then extend it to others: *attūpanāyika dhammapariyāya*.
Refrain, encourage others to refrain, and praise refraining.
The four factors of stream-entry.
sn55.7.living: This is the sutta to give anyone who asks what Buddhist ethics is, in one page.

sn55.37.title: Mahānāma on Lay Accomplishment
sn55.37.brief: What makes a lay follower accomplished in **virtue, faith, generosity and wisdom**? The precepts; faith in the Buddha's awakening; living at home with a heart free of stinginess, open-handed, devoted to charity, loving to give and share; and the wisdom that sees rise and fall.
teaching: The four lay accomplishments.
A classic description of a generous heart: *muttacāgo payatapāṇi vossaggarato yācayogo dānasaṃvibhāgarato*.

an3.65.title: The Kālāmas
an3.65.setting: Kesamutta, the town of the Kālāmas, who are confused by teachers each praising their own doctrine.
an3.65.brief: Do not go by oral tradition, lineage, testimony, scripture, logic, inference, reasoned thought, a favoured view, the speaker's apparent competence, or "this ascetic is our teacher". **When you know for yourselves** that things are unskilful, blameworthy, criticised by the wise and lead to harm, give them up. The Buddha then leads them to see this of greed, hatred and delusion, and teaches the divine abodes and the **four assurances**.
teaching: Ten unreliable grounds for belief.
The test: harm or benefit, praised or blamed by the wise, known for oneself.
The four assurances: if there is a next world, I go to a good place; if not, I live happily here; if evil befalls evildoers, I do none; if not, I am purified either way.

an8.21.title: Ugga of Vesālī
an8.21.setting: Vesālī. The Buddha praises the householder Ugga for eight wonderful qualities; a monk goes to ask Ugga what they are.
an8.21.brief: Ugga tells his own story: faith at first sight of the Buddha; awakening to the Dhamma; taking the precepts of celibacy and, with care and fairness, releasing his four young wives, giving one in marriage to the man she chose; sharing his wealth with the virtuous; serving monastics with respect; listening; not being elated when deities spoke to him; and being free of the five lower fetters.
teaching: A householder non-returner.
Wealth shared with the good.
Humility even in spiritual attainment.

an8.23.title: Hatthaka of Āḷavī
an8.23.setting: Āḷavī. The Buddha praises the householder Hatthaka for seven qualities.
an8.23.brief: Hatthaka has faith, virtue, conscience, prudence, learning, generosity and wisdom. When he hears the Buddha has praised him, he asks that no householder in white was present: he doesn't want praise. The Buddha adds an eighth quality: **modesty**.
teaching: The seven noble treasures, embodied.
The eighth: not wanting one's virtues known.

an9.20.title: Velāma
an9.20.setting: Sāvatthī. Anāthapiṇḍika says the alms his family gives are coarse.
an9.20.brief: The Buddha tells of the brahmin Velāma, his own past life, who gave an immense gift: gold, silver, elephants, chariots, cows. But more fruitful than that is feeding one person of right view; more again a stream-enterer, and so on up to a Buddha and the Saṅgha; a monastery; going for refuge; the precepts; **a moment of loving-kindness as long as it takes to pull a cow's udder**; and most fruitful of all, **perceiving impermanence for the time of a finger-snap**.
teaching: The scale of merit, from material gifts to insight.
Quality of recipient and quality of mind outweigh quantity.
Insight into impermanence crowns all giving.

an10.92.title: Dangers
an10.92.brief: A noble disciple who has calmed **five dangers and enmities** (killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying and intoxication), has the **four factors of stream-entry**, and has **seen and understood the noble method** (dependent origination) may declare themselves a stream-enterer.
teaching: Five fears and enmities: what the precepts protect against, here and hereafter.
The four factors.
Dependent origination as "the noble method" (*ariyo ñāyo*).

mn143.title: Advice to Anāthapiṇḍika
mn143.setting: Sāvatthī. Anāthapiṇḍika is gravely ill. Sāriputta and Ānanda visit.
mn143.brief: Sāriputta teaches him to cling to nothing: not the eye or what it sees, not consciousness, not the elements, not the aggregates, not this world or the next, nothing seen, heard, thought or known. Anāthapiṇḍika weeps: in all his years he has never heard such a teaching, and asks that householders be taught it too. He dies and is reborn in Tusita, and returns that night to praise Jetavana.
teaching: Non-clinging to every sense and every world.
"Let such talks be given to householders too: some have little dust in their eyes."
The great patron's death.

sn55.26.title: Anāthapiṇḍika Is Ill
sn55.26.setting: Sāvatthī. Sāriputta visits the sick householder.
sn55.26.brief: Sāriputta reminds him: you do not have the lack of faith, the bad conduct and wrong path factors that lead an ordinary person to the lower realms. You have confidence in the Buddha, Dhamma and Saṅgha, noble virtue, and right view through right freedom. As Anāthapiṇḍika reflects on this, his pain subsides.
teaching: Recollecting one's own good as medicine.
The bedside role of a spiritual friend.

sn55.40.title: Nandiya the Sakyan
sn55.40.brief: A stream-enterer can still be **negligent**: content with confidence and virtue, they make no further effort for seclusion and concentration, and their progress stalls. The diligent one goes further: joy, rapture, tranquillity, happiness, concentration, and the truths become clear.
teaching: Stream-entry is not a finish line.
Diligence (*appamāda*) carries one on.

sn55.54.title: Counselling the Sick
sn55.54.setting: Kapilavatthu. Mahānāma asks how a wise lay follower should counsel another wise lay follower who is gravely ill.
sn55.54.brief: A bedside method, step by step. First reassure them with the four kinds of confidence. Ask if they worry for their parents: they will die whether you worry or not. Their partner and children: the same. Then lead the mind upward: from human pleasures to divine ones, from the heavens to the Brahmā world, and from there to the ending of identity. Such a lay follower, the Buddha says, is no different from a monk freed by wisdom.
teaching: Reassure with the four factors.
Release worry for family.
Raise the mind, realm by realm, to letting go.
Lay liberation is equal to monastic liberation.
sn55.54.living: If you sit with the dying, this is your text. It is gentle, honest and practical, and it ends at the highest point.

an6.16.title: Nakula's Parents
an6.16.setting: Among the Bhaggas. Nakulapitā is gravely ill; his wife Nakulamātā sits by him.
an6.16.brief: She gives six reassurances so that he can die without worry: I can support the children by spinning; I will not take another husband; I will keep seeing the Buddha and the Saṅgha; I will keep the precepts; I will attain inner serenity; I am established in the Dhamma. He recovers, and the Buddha tells him he is fortunate to have such a wife.
teaching: A marriage as mutual spiritual support.
Six reassurances for a dying partner.
Worry is bad for the dying: the Buddha says it is painful to die anxious.

an6.119.title: Tapussa
an6.119.brief: The householder Tapussa, who with Bhallika was the first to take refuge in the Buddha after the awakening, has seen the deathless through six qualities: unwavering confidence in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Saṅgha, noble virtue, noble knowledge and noble freedom. The suttas that follow name many other lay people who reached the same.
teaching: Lay people realise the deathless.
Six qualities of a lay disciple who has seen the Dhamma.

mn54.title: Potaliya
mn54.setting: Āpaṇa, in Aṅguttarāpa. Potaliya, dressed as a renouncer, is offended at being called "householder": he has "cut off all affairs".
mn54.brief: The Buddha shows what cutting off affairs means in the noble discipline: eight kinds of abstention, from killing to arrogance. Then seven similes for sensual pleasures: a meatless bone thrown to a dog, a scrap of meat fought over by birds, a grass torch carried against the wind, a pit of coals, a dream, borrowed goods, a fruit tree others climb and cut. Then the jhānas and the three knowledges.
teaching: Renunciation is inner, not a costume.
Seven similes for sense pleasures, among the most vivid in the canon.

mn56.title: Upāli
mn56.setting: Nāḷandā. The wealthy Jain householder Upāli goes to refute the Buddha on whether physical or mental deeds are weightier.
mn56.brief: He is won over, and asks to become a follower. The Buddha tells him to think carefully, as a well-known man, and to keep giving to the Jains who depend on his family. Upāli is all the more inspired. When his former teacher comes, he praises the Buddha in a hundred epithets.
teaching: Mental intention is the weightiest kind of action.
Converts should keep supporting their former teachers: generosity is not sectarian.

sn42.2.title: The Actor
sn42.2.setting: Rājagaha. Tālapuṭa, the head of a theatre troupe, has heard that actors who make people laugh are reborn among the gods of laughter.
sn42.2.brief: The Buddha declines to answer twice. Pressed, he says: performers who inflame audiences already bound by greed, hatred and delusion, when they themselves are heedless, go to a hell, if they hold that wrong view. Tālapuṭa weeps, not at the answer but at having been deceived, and goes forth.
teaching: Art that inflames the defilements carries a cost.
The Buddha answers only when asked three times.

sn42.3.title: The Soldier
sn42.3.setting: Rājagaha. A professional warrior has heard that a soldier killed in battle is reborn in heaven.
sn42.3.brief: Pressed, the Buddha says: in battle the warrior's mind is already low and misdirected ("let these beings be killed, slaughtered, annihilated"); dying in that state, if he holds the heavenly view, he goes to a hell. The soldier weeps at having been deceived.
teaching: Intention at death matters.
No glory in killing.

sn42.6.title: The Western Brahmins
sn42.6.setting: Nāḷandā. A headman asks whether the Buddha, like the western brahmins, can raise the dead to heaven by ritual.
sn42.6.brief: Throw a heavy rock into a lake, and pray around it for it to float: it will not. So a wrongdoer will not rise because people pray. Pour ghee or oil into the lake and pray for it to sink: it will not. So the good rise by their own deeds.
teaching: Rites and prayers do not override kamma.
One's own conduct is what rises or sinks.

sn42.7.title: The Fields
sn42.7.setting: Nāḷandā. The headman asks why, if the Buddha has compassion for all, he teaches some more fully than others.
sn42.7.brief: A farmer has three fields: good, middling and poor. He sows the good one first, then the middling, and the poor one too, because it may at least yield cattle feed. So the Buddha teaches monastics, then lay followers, and even others who do not follow him: if they understand even a single line, it is for their long good.
teaching: Teaching for all, in order of readiness.
Even a single line can help.

sn42.8.title: The Conch Blower
sn42.8.setting: Nāḷandā. A Jain headman reports his teacher's view: whatever you do often decides your destiny.
sn42.8.brief: The Buddha shows the view is self-defeating, and that dwelling on past misdeeds only produces regret. The noble disciple instead gives up wrong deeds and spreads loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity in all directions, as a strong conch blower is heard in every quarter. Limited deeds do not remain beside such a boundless heart.
teaching: Remorse alone does not undo the past.
Boundless brahmavihāra outweighs limited deeds.

sn42.9.title: Families
sn42.9.setting: Nāḷandā, during a famine. The Jain leader sends a headman with a trap: does the Buddha not ruin families by going for alms in hard times?
sn42.9.brief: The Buddha says that in ninety-one aeons he knows of no family ruined by giving cooked alms. Rich families became rich through giving, truth and restraint. He names **eight causes of a family's ruin**: kings, thieves, fire, flood, lost buried treasure, failed businesses, a wastrel heir, and impermanence itself.
teaching: Giving does not ruin families.
Eight real causes of ruin, still recognisable today.

sn42.10.title: Maṇicūḷaka
sn42.10.setting: Rājagaha. In the royal court, some say Buddhist monks may accept gold and money. The headman Maṇicūḷaka disagrees, and asks the Buddha.
sn42.10.brief: The Buddha confirms: gold and money are not allowable for monastics. Anyone for whom they are allowable is allowed the five cords of sensual pleasure. What a monk needs, such as grass, wood or a cart, may be sought; money itself, never.
teaching: Monastics do not accept money.
Lay supporters provide requisites, not cash.

sn42.11.title: Bhadraka
sn42.11.setting: Uruvelakappa, among the Mallas. The headman asks about the origin and ending of suffering.
sn42.11.brief: Instead of a theory, the Buddha asks about his own life. Would he grieve if people in the town were killed or fined? Some, yes; others, no. Why the difference? Desire. And his son Ciravāsī, away from home: would he grieve if he died? "My life would be upset." And his wife: before he had seen or heard of her, did he have any love or desire for her? None. Suffering is rooted in desire.
teaching: Suffering arises from desire, as seen in our own loves.
The past, present and future are the same.

sn42.12.title: Rāsiya
sn42.12.setting: The headman Rāsiya asks whether the Buddha condemns all asceticism.
sn42.12.brief: The Buddha teaches the middle way between indulgence and self-mortification, then the ten kinds of people who enjoy sensual pleasures (as in AN 10.91), and three kinds of ascetics. Wealth honestly gained, enjoyed, shared and held without bondage is praised.
teaching: The middle way.
Ten kinds of wealth-users.
Wise and foolish austerity.

sn42.13.title: Pāṭaliya
sn42.13.setting: Uttara, among the Koliyans. The headman asks whether the Buddha knows magic.
sn42.13.brief: He does, but that does not make him a magician, as knowing a killer does not make one a killer. Pāṭaliya then reports many conflicting views he has heard. The Buddha teaches a practice beyond the dispute: give up wrongdoing and fill the world with the four divine abodes. Whichever view is true, such a person has thrown the winning dice.
teaching: Knowing evil is not doing it.
The "incontrovertible" practice: whatever the truth, the brahmavihāras win.

an3.36.title: The Divine Messengers
an3.36.brief: After death, King Yama questions a wrongdoer: did you not see the divine messengers? **A newborn child, an old person, a sick person, a criminal being punished, a corpse.** "Did you not think: I too am subject to birth, ageing, sickness and death; let me do good?" The deeds were yours, and you will experience the result.
teaching: Five messengers in ordinary life.
No one else made the deeds: not parents, friends, gods or ascetics.
The verses: the wise, seeing them, take up the Dhamma.

an5.57.title: Five Daily Reflections
an5.57.setting: Taught to the mendicants, and to "a woman or a man, a householder or a renunciant".
an5.57.brief: Five things to reflect on often: **I am subject to ageing; to sickness; to death; I will be separated from all that is dear; I am the owner and heir of my deeds.** Each one has a purpose: to cut the intoxication of youth, of health, of life, desire for the dear, and misconduct.
teaching: The five reflections, chanted daily in Theravāda monasteries.
Each answers a particular intoxication.
Extended to all beings, they lead to the path.
an5.57.living: Read these five lines every morning. They are not morbid; the Buddha says they make a person less reckless, less possessive and more careful with their actions.

an5.48.title: Things No One Can Have
an5.48.brief: Five things cannot be had by anyone, ascetic, brahmin, god, Māra or Brahmā: that what is subject to ageing should not age, sickness not sicken, death not die, ending not end, perishing not perish. The ordinary person, struck by these, grieves and is pierced by the arrow. The noble disciple reflects, "it is not only mine," and draws the arrow out.
teaching: Five unobtainable things.
Grief does not help: enemies rejoice, friends are pained.
Reflection removes the dart.

an3.39.title: Delicate
an3.39.brief: He was raised in luxury: lotus ponds, three palaces, Kāsi sandalwood, servants fed on rice and meat. Yet reflecting that he too would age, sicken and die, and that it was not fitting to be disgusted at others' ageing, he lost the **three intoxications: of youth, health and life**.
teaching: Privilege does not exempt anyone.
The three intoxications (*mada*).

sn22.1.title: Nakula's Father
sn22.1.setting: Among the Bhaggas. The aged Nakulapitā, often ill, asks for a teaching to support him.
sn22.1.brief: The Buddha: "Though my body is sick, my mind will not be sick." Sāriputta explains how: the ordinary person regards form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness as self, so when they change, the mind suffers. The noble disciple does not.
teaching: A sick body, a healthy mind.
Non-identification with the aggregates.

snp3.8.title: The Arrow
snp3.8.setting: The Sutta Nipāta. The commentary says it was taught to a layman grieving for a son.
snp3.8.brief: Life here is short and painful, and no means exists for the born not to die. As ripe fruit must fall, as clay pots break, so with mortals. Not by weeping is peace found; grief only harms the griever. Draw out the arrow of sorrow and you will find peace.
teaching: Death is certain for all.
Lamenting does not help the dead or the living.
"Pull out the arrow" (*abbahe sallam attano*).

ud8.8.title: Visākhā's Grandchild
ud8.8.setting: Sāvatthī. Visākhā comes in the middle of the day, clothes and hair wet: her beloved grandchild has died.
ud8.8.brief: Would she like to have as many children and grandchildren as there are people in Sāvatthī? Yes. And how many die in Sāvatthī each day? Many. Then she would never be without wet hair. Those with a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows; those with none have none.
teaching: Love and grief go together.
Freedom from sorrow is freedom from clinging, not from love's warmth.

mn97.title: Dhānañjāni
mn97.setting: Rājagaha. The brahmin Dhānañjāni has been robbing the king to support his family.
mn97.brief: Sāriputta asks: in hell, could you say "I did it for my parents, my wife, my children"? No. Family can be supported by righteous work. Later, as Dhānañjāni lies dying, Sāriputta teaches him the path to the Brahmā world through the four divine abodes. The Buddha says he could have taught him more.
teaching: Family duty never excuses wrongdoing.
Honest livelihood is enough to support a family.
At the deathbed, aim high.

sn47.29.title: Sirivaḍḍha
sn47.29.setting: Rājagaha. The householder Sirivaḍḍha is ill and asks Ānanda to visit.
sn47.29.brief: Ānanda teaches him to practise the four establishments of mindfulness. He answers that he already does, and that he has given up the five lower fetters. Ānanda declares him a non-returner.
teaching: Lay meditators reach high attainment.
Mindfulness as the practice of the sick.

snp1.8.title: The Discourse on Loving-kindness
snp1.8.setting: The Sutta Nipāta and the Khuddakapāṭha. The commentary tells of monks who went to a forest for the rains and were frightened by the tree deities; the Buddha sent them back with this discourse.
snp1.8.brief: The best-known text of the Theravāda world. It opens with the qualities of one who wants to reach peace: capable, upright, gentle, humble, content, easy to support, of few duties, light in living, calm in the senses. It then pours out the wish: may all beings be happy, seen and unseen, near and far, born and to be born. As a mother would protect her only child with her life, so one should cultivate a boundless heart toward all beings.
teaching: **The foundation:** fifteen qualities of conduct before the meditation begins.
**The wish:** *sukhino vā khemino hontu, sabbe sattā bhavantu sukhitattā*.
**The method:** pervading beings of every size and kind, then every direction, without obstruction, hatred or enmity.
**The posture:** standing, walking, sitting or lying down, as long as one is awake: this is called the divine abiding here.
**The end:** not grasping at views, virtuous, with vision, free of sensual greed, one does not come again to a womb.

an11.15.title: The Eleven Benefits of Loving-kindness
an11.15.brief: When the heart's release by loving-kindness is cultivated, developed, made a vehicle and a basis, eleven benefits follow.
teaching: Sleep at ease; wake at ease; no bad dreams.
Dear to humans; dear to non-humans; protected by deities.
Fire, poison and weapons do not harm you.
The mind quickly becomes concentrated; the face is serene.
You die unconfused; and if you go no further, you are reborn in the Brahmā world.

an8.1.title: Eight Benefits of Loving-kindness
an8.1.brief: The eight-fold version of the benefits, with verses: one who develops mettā even for a single being becomes good; for all beings, a noble one makes abundant merit. Kings who conquered the earth with great sacrifices are not worth a sixteenth part of a heart well developed in love.
teaching: Sleep and wake at ease, no bad dreams, dear to humans and non-humans, protected by deities, safe from fire, poison and weapons, Brahmā world.
"Not worth a sixteenth part of a mind well developed in love."

sn20.3.title: Families
sn20.3.brief: Families with many women and few men are easily attacked by bandits. A meditator who does not develop loving-kindness is easily attacked by non-human beings. Families with few women and many men are hard to attack; so is one who develops mettā.
teaching: Mettā as protection.

iti27.title: Loving-kindness Outshines All Merit
iti27.brief: All the grounds for making merit are not worth a sixteenth part of the heart's release by loving-kindness. It outshines them, as moonlight outshines the stars, as the autumn sun outshines the sky, as the morning star blazes at dawn.
teaching: Mettā is the brightest merit.
Three similes of light.

an4.125.title: Loving-kindness and Rebirth
an4.125.brief: Someone who dwells pervading the world with loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity enjoys it and may be reborn among the gods of the Brahmā realms, for an aeon or more. An ordinary person, when that life ends, may fall to lower realms; a disciple of the Buddha is fully extinguished in that very existence.
teaching: The divine abodes lead to the Brahmā realms.
Insight makes the difference between temporary and final peace.

mn7.title: The Simile of the Cloth
mn7.brief: A dirty cloth will not take the dye; a clean one will. So a defiled mind leads to a bad destination, a clean mind to a good one. The Buddha lists sixteen defilements, from greed to negligence. Purified, with confidence in the Triple Gem, joy arises, then the four divine abodes. To the brahmin Sundarika, who believes in sacred rivers, he says: bathe here, in kindness to all beings.
teaching: Sixteen defilements of mind (*upakkilesa*).
Confidence in the Triple Gem as a source of joy.
The four divine abodes.
"The inner bathing."

dn13.title: The Three Knowledges
dn13.setting: Manasākaṭa, Kosala. The young brahmins Vāseṭṭha and Bhāradvāja argue about which teacher shows the true path to Brahmā.
dn13.brief: The Buddha asks: has any of these teachers, or their teachers back to the seventh generation, seen Brahmā? No. Then it is a line of blind men holding each other, a staircase built to a palace no one has seen, a man calling on the far bank of a river to come over. The way to companionship with Brahmā is the gradual path: virtue, abandoning the hindrances, and the four divine abodes, pervading the world "as a strong conch blower is heard in all four directions".
teaching: Authority without experience is empty.
The brahmavihāras as the path to Brahmā.
The conch-blower simile.

mn118.title: Mindfulness of Breathing
mn118.setting: Sāvatthī, the Eastern Monastery, the full-moon night of the Pavāraṇā. The Buddha is so pleased with the monks' practice that he extends the retreat to the Komudī full moon of Kattika.
mn118.brief: The fullest teaching on breath meditation: **sixteen steps in four sets of four**, mapped onto the four establishments of mindfulness, which fulfil the seven factors of awakening, which fulfil knowledge and freedom.
teaching: **Body:** long breath, short breath, experiencing the whole body, calming the bodily formation.
**Feeling:** experiencing rapture, happiness, the mental formation, calming it.
**Mind:** experiencing the mind, gladdening it, concentrating it, freeing it.
**Dhammas:** contemplating impermanence, fading, cessation, letting go.
Breath → four satipaṭṭhāna → seven bojjhaṅga → knowledge and freedom.

sn54.1.title: One Thing
sn54.1.brief: One thing, developed and cultivated, is of great fruit: mindfulness of breathing. Here is the method in its simplest canonical form. Go to a forest, the root of a tree or an empty hut; sit cross-legged, body straight; establish mindfulness in front of you; mindful, breathe in, mindful, breathe out. Then the sixteen steps.
teaching: The setting, the posture, the attention.
The sixteen steps in brief.

sn54.13.title: Ānanda on the Breath
sn54.13.setting: Sāvatthī. Ānanda asks whether one thing fulfils four, four fulfil seven, and seven fulfil two.
sn54.13.brief: Yes: **mindfulness of breathing** fulfils the **four establishments of mindfulness**; these fulfil the **seven factors of awakening**; these fulfil **knowledge and freedom**. The awakening factors are developed in dependence on seclusion, dispassion and cessation, ripening in letting go.
teaching: 1 → 4 → 7 → 2: the architecture of the path in breath.

mn62.title: The Longer Advice to Rāhula
mn62.setting: Sāvatthī. The young Rāhula, walking for alms behind the Buddha, admires his own body; the Buddha turns and tells him to see all form as not-self.
mn62.brief: Sāriputta later tells Rāhula to practise breath meditation. When Rāhula asks how, the Buddha first teaches the five elements as not-self, then **meditation like the earth** (which is not troubled by what is thrown on it), water, fire, air and space; then the four divine abodes, foulness and impermanence; and finally the sixteen steps of breathing, ending: "even the final breaths are known as they cease."
teaching: The elements meditation as preparation.
Meditate like the earth.
A complete course in one sutta.

an10.60.title: Girimānanda
an10.60.setting: Sāvatthī. Venerable Girimānanda is gravely ill; the Buddha sends Ānanda with ten perceptions to recite.
an10.60.brief: Ten perceptions: impermanence, not-self, foulness, drawbacks (a long list of diseases the body is subject to), giving up, fading away, cessation, disenchantment with the whole world, impermanence of all conditions, and **mindfulness of breathing** with its sixteen steps. Hearing them, Girimānanda recovers. It is chanted as pirith for the sick.
teaching: Ten perceptions (*dasa saññā*).
The body's many illnesses, named.
A complete breath meditation within a healing chant.

mn10.title: The Establishments of Mindfulness
mn10.brief: "This is the direct path for the purification of beings": the four establishments of mindfulness. Observing the body in the body, feelings in feelings, mind in mind and dhammas in dhammas, ardent, aware and mindful, free of desire and aversion for the world. Practised for seven years, or even seven days, it leads to awakening or non-return.
teaching: **Body:** breathing, postures, full awareness in activities, thirty-one parts, four elements, nine charnel-ground contemplations.
**Feelings:** pleasant, painful, neutral; worldly and unworldly.
**Mind:** with or without greed, hatred, delusion; contracted, expanded, concentrated, freed.
**Dhammas:** hindrances, aggregates, sense bases, awakening factors, four noble truths.
Internally, externally, both; arising and passing; "mindfulness established just enough for knowledge."

mn119.title: Mindfulness of the Body
mn119.setting: Sāvatthī. The monks are talking about how wonderful the Buddha's teaching on body mindfulness is.
mn119.brief: The body contemplations of MN 10, followed by the four jhānas with their similes, all as "mindfulness of the body". Whoever develops it includes all skilful qualities, as one who imagines the ocean includes all the rivers that flow into it. Ten benefits follow, from mastering discontent and fear to the ending of the defilements.
teaching: Body practices as a gateway to jhāna.
Similes: a heavy stone ball on wet clay (Māra finds a way in) and a ball of string on a wooden board (he does not).
Ten benefits.

snp1.11.title: Victory
snp1.11.setting: The Sutta Nipāta. The commentary says it was taught to the nun Rūpanandā and others who prided themselves on beauty.
snp1.11.brief: Walking, standing, sitting or lying down, the body bends and stretches. It is bound together by bones and sinews, smeared with skin and flesh, and filled with things the fool regards as beautiful. Its nine openings ooze constantly. And when it lies dead, swollen, livid, cast away in a charnel ground, dogs and jackals feed on it. "As this is, so is that": the wise see their own body in the dead one.
teaching: Contemplation of the body's parts and of death.
"As this is, so is that; as that is, so is this."
The cure for vanity and lust.

sn47.19.title: The Acrobat
sn47.19.brief: An acrobat tells his apprentice: you watch me and I will watch you, and we will come down safely. The apprentice says: you look after yourself, and I will look after myself. The Buddha sides with the apprentice. **Looking after yourself, you look after others; looking after others, you look after yourself.** The first is mindfulness; the second is patience, harmlessness, love and kindness.
teaching: Mindfulness protects oneself and others.
Kindness protects others and oneself.

sn47.20.title: The Most Beautiful Girl in the Land
sn47.20.brief: A huge crowd gathers to watch the finest dancer and singer in the country. A man is told to carry a bowl brimful of oil between the crowd and the performer, with a man behind him holding a raised sword, ready to cut off his head if a single drop spills. Would he become heedless? The bowl is **mindfulness of the body**.
teaching: A simile for undistracted attention amid temptation.

an6.10.title: The Six Recollections
an6.10.setting: Kapilavatthu. Mahānāma asks how a noble disciple who has understood the teaching mostly dwells.
an6.10.brief: They recollect **the Buddha** (*iti pi so bhagavā…*), **the Dhamma** (*svākkhāto…*), **the Saṅgha** (*supaṭipanno…*), **their own virtue**, **their own generosity**, and **the deities**: "the faith, virtue, learning, generosity and wisdom that brought them there, I have too." When they do, the mind is not overcome by greed, hatred or delusion; it is straight, and from it come joy, rapture, tranquillity, happiness and concentration.
teaching: The full formulas of the three recollections of the Triple Gem.
Recollecting one's own virtue and generosity as a meditation.
The sequence: gladness → rapture → tranquillity → happiness → samādhi.

an11.11.title: Mahānāma (1)
an11.11.setting: Kapilavatthu, at the end of the rains. Mahānāma learns the Buddha will soon set out and asks how he should live while apart.
an11.11.brief: Five qualities to rely on (faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom) and then the six recollections, each described in full with its fruit: a straight mind, joy, rapture, tranquillity, happiness and concentration.
teaching: Practise these while walking, standing, sitting, lying down, at work, and at home with a house full of children.

an11.12.title: Mahānāma (2)
an11.12.brief: The same question and teaching, with the explicit instruction that these recollections are to be developed in every posture, while busy at work, and while lying in a bed crowded with children: the canon's clearest statement that this is a householder's meditation.
teaching: A practice for busy lay life.

sn11.3.title: The Crest of the Banner
sn11.3.setting: Sāvatthī. The Buddha tells of the war between gods and titans: Sakka told his troops that if they felt fear, they should look up at his banner.
sn11.3.brief: If you are afraid in a forest, at the root of a tree or in an empty hut, recollect the Buddha; or the Dhamma; or the Saṅgha. Fear and terror will vanish. Sakka's banner may fail, because Sakka is not free of greed, hatred and delusion; the Buddha is.
teaching: The three recollections as a remedy for fear.
A principal paritta of the Sri Lankan tradition.

an6.19.title: Mindfulness of Death (1)
an6.19.brief: The Buddha asks the monks how they practise mindfulness of death. "If I could live a day and night…", "a day…", "for one meal…", "for four or five mouthfuls…". Only those who say "for one mouthful" and "for a single in-and-out breath" practise it diligently. The others are negligent.
teaching: Measure life in breaths, not years.
Urgency without fear.

an6.20.title: Mindfulness of Death (2)
